author: reek
body: It used to commit a SECOND directory entry under the same name. fat16-find-free-slot answers the first free slot and knows nothing about names, so the second write claimed a fresh cluster chain and wrote a second entry; readers take whichever they meet first, which is the older one sitting in the lower slot. The write answered True, the clusters were really spent, and the file still read back its previous contents. fat16-create-directory has guarded against exactly this since it was written; files never got the same guard.

author: reek
body: The read-back after the second write is the whole test, and the reason is that the obvious assertion is the one that cannot fail. A test that wrote twice and checked the write ANSWERED True passed before this fix and after it. A test that checked the file still held its first contents passed before the fix for the bug's reason and after it for no reason at all. Only demanding the NEW contents separates them, and before the fix this line read "first".

author: reek
body: The root and a subdirectory are both exercised because they reach the disk through different slot finders -- fat16-find-free-slot for the root and fat16-find-or-grow-slot-in-dir for a chain -- and the defect was in both. Fixing one and shipping it as fixed is the shape of failure this battery is supposed to make hard.

author: reek
body: The listing counts are the leak half, and they are what the read-back alone cannot see. A replacement that wrote the new bytes but still added an entry would return the right contents from the newer entry and grow the directory every time it was written. One name written three times must leave exactly one entry behind it.
